newsitem.title: japan: Gore visit eases Japan's worries about bases.
newsitem.headline: Gore visit eases Japan's worries about bases.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore wrapped up a visit to Japan on Monday that eased both nations' worries about cutbacks in American military forces in Asia.

Gore was forthright in stating the United States wanted to maintain its present troop levels in Japan and the rest of Asia, while Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was equally firm in saying he would not give in to groups which want U.S. bases in Japan shut.

During his 24 hours in Japan, part of an Asian tour that also includes China and South Korea, Gore delivered a speech to an environmental conference and in general made it clear that Japan remained the United States' key ally in Asia.

Although the main focus of Gore's trip to East Asia is the four days he spends in China, his talks with Japanese officials cleared away any lingering worries about Japan's future as the United States' main military base in Asia.
"The Japan-U.S. alliance is the foundation for peace and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region," Hashimoto told reporters after an hour-long meeting with Gore.
"It is our responsibility to provide land and facilities (to the U.S. military) in a stable and smooth manner," he added.

Prior to leaving for Beijing on Monday afternoon, Gore told 1,000 U.S. military personnel and family members at a U.S. Air Force base on the outskirts of Tokyo: "The peace and security of the Pacific region rest on your backs."
The U.S. military, Gore said, "are a stabilising force in a region of the world that has become vitally important to the United States".

Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, which Tokyo strongly opposes. The 47,000 make up half of U.S. forces in Asia.
On Sunday, Hashimoto chose the day of Gore's arrival to announce he planned to push through parliament a new law to seek continued leases on private land used by U.S. bases on Okinawa.
Gore was equally adamant in his comments that Washington did not want changes in troop levels in Japan.
Asked on Sunday if the current force can be reduced over the next decade, Gore replied: "I think we need them now and for the foreseeable future.
"In my view, this would be the worst time to have some reduction in U.S. forces here," Gore said.
In an arrival statement on Sunday, Gore said his visit was meant to reaffirm America's commitment to the region.
"The security and prosperity of the United States is vitally tied to the Asia-Pacific region," Gore said.
Both the United States and Japan agree that China is the key to peace in Asia and hope to draw Beijing into dialogue on all issues involving the region.
In a speech at an environmental conference, Gore called for the world's nations to agree to legally binding targets for limiting greenhouse gas emissions when they meet in Japan in December.

"The growth of our economies and the stability of our societies are intertwined with the effects of climate change, environmental degradation, resource depletion, threats to human health, and population shifts... Our success will depend upon far-sighted wisdom in our choices," he said.
Gore said the United States sees three essential ingredients to a successful outcome of an environmental summit scheduled for Kyoto, western Japan, in December.
"First, the developed world must agree to realistic and achievable legally binding targets for greenhouse gas emissions," he said.
"At the same time, we must take care to develop targets that put us on a more sustainable energy path without sacrificing continued economic growth and development," Gore said.

At the last summit -- the so-called Rio de Janeiro Earth summit in Brazil in 1992 -- then U.S. president George Bush backed targets for limiting greenhouse gases, but refused to accept legally binding targets.
Gore called for maximum flexibility to ensure governments were given every opportunity to meet their commitments.
The third element, Gore said, was to acknowledge the global nature of the problem of protecting the environment.
